cases.title: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration
cases.stem: Mrs. Nisha Kapoor is a 25-year-old primigravida at 10 weeks of pregnancy who presents to the antenatal unit with persistent nausea and vomiting for the last several days. She reports that she is unable to tolerate food and has kept down only small sips of water. She feels dizzy on standing, has a dry mouth, and says her clothes feel loose because she has been losing weight. On assessment, the nurse notes blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, pulse 112 beats per minute, dry mucous membranes, dark concentrated urine, and visible fatigue. The patient says, “I wanted this pregnancy so much, but I feel miserable and weak all the time.” The nurse suspects hyperemesis gravidarum rather than normal morning sickness. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings most strongly support hyperemesis gravidarum rather than common nausea of pregnancy? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tachycardia and low blood pressure
Dizziness and weakness
Persistent vomiting with poor intake
Dark concentrated urine
Dry mucous membranes

questions.rationale: All these cues point to clinically significant fluid volume deficit rather than ordinary early-pregnancy nausea. Hyperemesis gravidarum is characterised by persistent vomiting, dehydration, weight loss, and hemodynamic changes. Dark urine and dry mucous membranes indicate poor hydration, while tachycardia and hypotension suggest the body is compensating for low circulating volume. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s priority interpretation of this presentation?

options.text: Hyperemesis gravidarum with dehydration and risk of electrolyte imbalance
Normal first-trimester discomfort that can be managed by reassurance alone
Labour-related abdominal pain
A psychiatric cause of vomiting with no obstetric significance

questions.rationale: This patient’s findings show more than common morning sickness. The signs of dehydration and likely electrolyte loss make this an obstetric and medical concern. NCLEX reasoning requires distinguishing expected pregnancy discomforts from findings that threaten maternal wellbeing and fetal support. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem should the nurse prioritise first?

options.text: Fear related to pregnancy adjustment
Disturbed body image
Knowledge deficit regarding infant care
Deficient fluid volume related to persistent vomiting

questions.rationale: Although emotional support is important, the most urgent issue is fluid deficit. Dehydration can quickly worsen maternal perfusion, renal function, and nutritional status, which in turn may compromise pregnancy progress. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage the patient to eat a heavy meal immediately
Delay intervention until the next prenatal visit
Begin focused assessment of hydration status, support rest, and prepare for fluid replacement and antiemetic therapy as prescribed
Tell the patient that vomiting is normal and she should go home

questions.rationale: Immediate nursing care should focus on hydration, safety, and preparation for treatment. Forcing a heavy meal is unrealistic and may worsen symptoms. Sending the patient home without treatment would ignore signs of dehydration and clinical deterioration. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor intake and output closely
Observe for worsening dizziness or electrolyte-related weakness
Reassess weight trends and urine concentration
Provide nonjudgmental support and explain the condition
Ignore emotional distress because physical issues are the only priority

questions.rationale: NGN-level maternity care includes both physical and emotional support. Intake/output and weight trends help evaluate hydration and nutrition. Emotional reassurance matters because prolonged vomiting can be frightening and discouraging. Ignoring distress would not reflect holistic nursing care. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Hyperemesis Gravidarum with Dehydration | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the plan of care is effective?

options.text: The patient tolerates fluids better, urine becomes less concentrated, pulse slows, and dizziness decreases
Vomiting worsens and the patient becomes more hypotensive
The nurse stops monitoring after one dose of antiemetic
The patient remains unable to take in fluids but says she feels hopeful

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by better hydration, less concentrated urine, more stable vital signs, and reduced dizziness. Hopefulness is valuable, but physiological improvement is the clearest outcome indicator.

cases.title: Severe Preeclampsia
cases.stem: Mrs. Farah Ahmed is a 31-year-old woman at 34 weeks’ gestation who presents to the labour assessment unit complaining of a severe frontal headache, blurred vision, and sudden swelling of her hands and face. She reports that the baby has been moving, but she feels unusually unwell and says, “My head feels like it will burst.” Assessment reveals blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, brisk reflexes, +3 protein on dipstick, and mild right upper quadrant discomfort. The fetal monitor is applied, and the nurse recognises that this pattern is concerning for severe preeclampsia with risk of maternal and fetal deterioration. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Severe Preeclampsia | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are red flags for severe preeclampsia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Severe headache
Right upper quadrant discomfort
Blood pressure 168/112 mmHg
Visual disturbance
Proteinuria and brisk reflexes

questions.rationale: All of these are classic warning signs of severe preeclampsia. Headache, visual disturbance, and hypertension suggest cerebral involvement. Brisk reflexes indicate increased neuromuscular irritability, and right upper quadrant pain may reflect hepatic involvement. NCLEX-style maternity questions place heavy emphasis on recognising these as urgent findings. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Severe Preeclampsia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of this presentation?

options.text: Severe preeclampsia with risk of seizure, placental compromise, and maternal organ injury
Normal third-trimester discomforts
Early postpartum haemorrhage
Simple anxiety about labour

questions.rationale: The symptom cluster is highly concerning for severe preeclampsia. This is not an expected discomfort of pregnancy. The nurse must think about maternal cerebral, renal, hepatic, and placental risks. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Severe Preeclampsia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Disturbed sleep pattern
Risk for maternal seizure and reduced placental perfusion
Knowledge deficit regarding breastfeeding
Anxiety about motherhood

questions.rationale: The priority is prevention of maternal and fetal injury. Preeclampsia threatens the brain, liver, kidneys, and uteroplacental circulation. That risk overrides all long-term teaching needs. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Severe Preeclampsia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage the patient to walk around to reduce swelling
Delay intervention until laboratory results return next day
Offer a large meal and discharge home
Reduce stimulation, maintain safety, initiate close maternal-fetal monitoring, and prepare for urgent antihypertensive and magnesium sulfate therapy as prescribed

questions.rationale: The nurse must reduce seizure risk, support close monitoring, and prepare for time-sensitive management. Walking, discharge, or delay would be unsafe. In severe preeclampsia, nursing priorities include seizure precautions, fetal assessment, and readiness for urgent escalation. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Severe Preeclampsia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor reflexes, respiratory status, and urine output closely if magnesium sulfate is started
Prepare for possible urgent birth if maternal or fetal status worsens
Maintain a calm, low-stimulation environment
Dismiss blurred vision because oedema alone explains it
Assess fetal heart rate patterns and maternal symptoms frequently

questions.rationale: Magnesium sulfate monitoring is critical because toxicity can depress respirations. Fetal monitoring remains essential because placental perfusion may be impaired. Visual changes should never be dismissed in preeclampsia. Anticipating possible urgent delivery reflects advanced clinical judgment. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Severe Preeclampsia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement or stabilisation?

options.text: Headache intensifies and blood pressure rises further
Fetal monitoring is discontinued because the mother feels calmer
Blood pressure becomes better controlled, severe headache lessens, reflexes are appropriately monitored, and fetal status remains reassuring
Respirations fall dangerously on magnesium sulfate without reassessment

questions.rationale: Stabilisation is shown by improved blood pressure, reduced neurological symptoms, and continued maternal-fetal monitoring. Respiratory depression or worsening hypertension would indicate poor control or complications.

cases.title: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission
cases.stem: Mrs. Simran Kaur is a 29-year-old woman at 35 weeks’ gestation admitted earlier in the day with severe preeclampsia. While the nurse is updating observations, the patient suddenly becomes rigid and begins to seize in bed. Her partner panics and calls for help. The fetal monitor is in place, the room has low lighting, and side rails are raised. The nurse must protect the mother from injury, support airway safety, and prepare for emergency management while recognising that fetal compromise may also occur during the event. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: What makes this an obstetric emergency? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pregnancy at 35 weeks
Tonic-clonic seizure activity
Possible fetal compromise during maternal seizure
Known severe preeclampsia
Maternal risk of airway compromise and trauma

questions.rationale: A seizure in a patient with severe preeclampsia is eclampsia, a life-threatening obstetric emergency. Pregnancy context is important, but what makes the situation emergent is the direct risk to maternal airway, oxygenation, circulation, and fetal wellbeing. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the nurse’s priority interpretation?

options.text: The patient is having a normal labour event
The patient only needs comfort measures
The patient is experiencing eclampsia requiring immediate seizure management and maternal-fetal stabilisation
The seizure can be ignored until it stops

questions.rationale: This is eclampsia and must be treated urgently. NCLEX expects immediate recognition of seizure risk in hypertensive pregnancy complications and rapid implementation of emergency priorities. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent during the seizure?

options.text: Airway obstruction, maternal injury, and decreased oxygen delivery to mother and fetus
Need for postpartum teaching
Anxiety about labour pain
Disturbed sleep pattern

questions.rationale: During active seizure, the greatest danger is compromise of maternal airway, oxygenation, and physical safety. The fetus is also vulnerable if maternal oxygen delivery drops. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Try to hold the patient down forcefully
Leave the room to find the doctor before doing anything else
Stay with the patient, protect from injury, position for airway safety as feasible after the seizure, call for urgent help, and prepare prescribed seizure management
Put an object in the patient’s mouth to prevent tongue injury

questions.rationale: The nurse must remain with the patient, protect from injury, and support airway safety. Objects should never be forced into the mouth. Forceful restraint can injure the patient. Leaving the room without first ensuring active response and protection would be unsafe. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate after the seizure subsides? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain seizure precautions and low stimulation
Reassess airway, breathing, circulation, and maternal level of consciousness
Assess fetal status and continue close monitoring
Assume no further assessment is needed once the shaking stops
Prepare for magnesium sulfate or review of ongoing magnesium therapy as ordered

questions.rationale: Post-seizure care includes full maternal reassessment, fetal reassessment, seizure prevention strategies, and medication management. The end of visible seizure activity does not mean the emergency has ended. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Eclampsia During Antepartum Admission | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that immediate nursing management is effective?

options.text: The nurse documents only the duration without reassessment
Fetal status is ignored because the seizure is over
The patient remains unmonitored after the seizure ends
The mother is protected from injury, airway is maintained, maternal status is reassessed, and fetal monitoring resumes appropriately

questions.rationale: Effective care includes protection during the seizure and comprehensive reassessment afterward. Both mother and fetus require continued evaluation.

cases.title: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding
cases.stem: Mrs. Elena D’Souza is a 33-year-old woman at 32 weeks’ gestation who presents with sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She denies abdominal pain or contractions and says the baby has been moving normally. She appears frightened and asks whether her baby is in danger. Her blood pressure is 110/68 mmHg, pulse 102 beats per minute, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, and the bleeding continues lightly onto the pad. The nurse suspects placenta previa and understands that some common examination approaches are unsafe until the placenta location is confirmed. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings are most consistent with placenta previa? Select all that apply.

options.text: Absence of abdominal pain
Ongoing fetal movement
Painless bleeding
Bright-red vaginal bleeding
Third-trimester presentation

questions.rationale: Placenta previa typically presents with painless bright-red bleeding in the second half of pregnancy. Fetal movement may still be present, especially if fetal compromise has not yet developed. The absence of pain helps distinguish it from placental abruption in many cases. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Postpartum haemorrhage
Likely placenta previa requiring maternal-fetal assessment and bleeding precautions
Placental abruption with severe pain
Normal labour show

questions.rationale: The bleeding pattern strongly suggests placenta previa. Because placenta overlies or approaches the cervical os, vaginal bleeding may occur without pain. The nurse must think about safe assessment and preventing further bleeding. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Knowledge deficit about newborn sleep
Readiness for discharge
Disturbed body image
Risk for maternal blood loss and fetal compromise related to placental bleeding

questions.rationale: The immediate concern is ongoing bleeding and its impact on maternal circulation and fetal perfusion. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Assess maternal-fetal status, monitor bleeding, and avoid vaginal examination until placenta location is confirmed by the appropriate team
Perform a digital vaginal exam to check dilation
Delay fetal monitoring until bleeding stops
Encourage the patient to walk around

questions.rationale: In suspected placenta previa, digital vaginal examination may provoke severe bleeding and is contraindicated unless specifically directed in a controlled setting. Maternal and fetal monitoring are immediate priorities. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Monitor vital signs and bleeding amount closely
Explain the need for pelvic rest if ordered
Prepare for ultrasound-based evaluation and possible admission
Ignore maternal anxiety because bleeding is the only priority
Apply fetal monitoring and assess fetal status

questions.rationale: Maternity care is both physiological and supportive. Monitoring, fetal assessment, preparation for evaluation, and patient teaching are all appropriate. Anxiety should not be ignored. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placenta Previa with Third-Trimester Bleeding | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates stable management at this stage?

options.text: A digital exam is performed without indication
Bleeding decreases or remains controlled, maternal vital signs stay stable, and fetal status remains reassuring
The patient is discharged without ongoing assessment
Bleeding increases while monitoring is reduced

questions.rationale: Stable maternal signs and reassuring fetal assessment indicate the situation is under better control, though continued vigilance is still needed.

cases.title: Placental Abruption
cases.stem: Mrs. Priya Menon, a 37-year-old multiparous woman at 35 weeks’ gestation, arrives complaining of sudden severe abdominal pain and dark vaginal bleeding after she slipped on wet flooring earlier in the day. She is guarding her abdomen and says the pain is constant. She reports reduced fetal movement since the pain began. On assessment, the uterus feels firm and tender. Blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg, pulse 124 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and the fetal monitor shows a concerning pattern. The nurse suspects placental abruption. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placental Abruption | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support placental abruption? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dark vaginal bleeding
Uterine tenderness and firmness
Reduced fetal movement
Signs of maternal instability
Severe abdominal pain

questions.rationale: Placental abruption typically presents with painful bleeding, uterine tenderness, and often reduced fetal movement due to compromised placental exchange. Maternal tachycardia and hypotension suggest significant blood loss or shock. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placental Abruption | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Baby blues
Normal labour discomfort
Placental abruption with risk of maternal haemorrhage and fetal compromise
Placenta previa

questions.rationale: This is a painful bleeding emergency, unlike the typically painless bleeding seen with placenta previa. The nurse must recognise the dual risk to mother and fetus. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placental Abruption | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Impaired placental perfusion with maternal haemorrhage risk
Knowledge deficit about parenting
Disturbed sleep pattern
Need for menu planning

questions.rationale: Placental separation compromises fetal oxygenation and may lead to severe maternal bleeding. This is a high-priority obstetric emergency. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placental Abruption | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay fetal monitoring until the bleeding is measured for several hours
Encourage the patient to walk to the toilet
Offer oral food and fluids first
Initiate urgent maternal-fetal assessment, support circulation, and prepare for emergency obstetric management

questions.rationale: The nurse must stabilise maternal circulation and monitor fetal status immediately. Delay or unnecessary activity would be unsafe. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placental Abruption | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Preparation for urgent birth if maternal or fetal instability worsens
Continuous fetal heart rate assessment
Maintaining IV access and readiness for rapid intervention as ordered
Frequent monitoring of maternal vital signs and bleeding
Assuming that reduced fetal movement is not important

questions.rationale: Reduced fetal movement is highly significant and should not be ignored. The nurse must prepare for escalation and possible urgent delivery. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Placental Abruption | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates the patient is being effectively stabilised while definitive care is arranged?

options.text: Monitoring is stopped because pain is present
Bleeding increases without reassessment
Maternal perfusion is supported, fetal status is continuously assessed, and the team is prepared for rapid obstetric intervention
The patient is left alone because the doctor has been called

questions.rationale: Effective emergency nursing care involves continuous assessment, support, and anticipation of urgent obstetric management.
